property_summary: For any caller who is the owner and any contract balance, calling withdrawAll() transfers the full contract balance out (leaving address(c).balance == 0); the mutant that sends only half breaks this by leaving a nonzero balance for some input balances.

For any nonzero contract balance and when the owner calls withdrawAll(), the reference contract empties the contract (address(c).balance == 0) after the call; the mutant that withdraws only half will leave a nonzero balance for some balances, violating this rule.

For any nonzero initial contract balance and when the owner calls withdrawAll(), the reference contract reduces the contract balance by exactly the amount transferred to the owner (i.e., the owner's received increase equals the decrease in address(c).balance); the mutant that withdraws only half can cause a mismatch between the owner's balance change and the contract balance decrease (they won't match) for some input balances.

For any nonzero initial contract balance and when the owner calls withdrawAll(), the reference contract transfers exactly the prior contract balance to the owner (so address(c).balance becomes 0); the mutant that sends only half will leave address(c).balance > 0 for some initial balances, violating this rule (we will restrict to owner-caller and nonzero deposits but keep domain wide).

For every initial nonzero contract balance funded by any sender, when the owner calls withdrawAll() the reference contract transfers the entire contract balance out leaving address(c).balance == 0; the mutant that withdraws only half will for some fuzzed initial balances leave address(c).balance != 0, violating this rule.

For any caller who is the owner and any contract balance > 0, calling withdrawAll transfers the full contract balance out (reducing address(c).balance to 0); the mutant that calls withdraw(0) breaks this by leaving balance unchanged for some inputs.

For any owner caller and any nonzero contract balance, calling withdrawAll transfers the entire contract balance out (leaving address(c).balance == 0); the mutant that calls withdraw(0) can leave the balance nonzero, violating this property for some inputs.

For any owner caller and any initial contract balance B > 0, after owner calls withdrawAll the reference reduces address(c).balance by exactly B (i.e., to 0); the mutant that calls withdraw(0) can leave the balance unchanged, so there exists some owner and B>0 where address(c).balance remains >0 after withdrawAll.

If the owner calls withdrawAll after the contract has a positive balance, the call must forward a nonzero amount to the owner (so either the call succeeds transferring >0 and reduces address(c).balance, or it reverts); the mutant that calls withdraw(0) can succeed while transferring 0 and leaving balance unchanged, violating this rule.

For any caller that is the owner and any positive contract balance, calling withdrawAll causes the contract's balance to become zero (the reference transfers out the full balance); the mutant that calls withdraw(0) can leave the contract balance nonzero for some inputs.

For every caller and balance, calling withdrawAll only succeeds (transfers the contract balance and leaves contract balance zero) when invoked by the owner; the mutant inverts the ownership check so some non-owner caller can successfully withdraw and make address(c).balance become zero while the owner cannot — the property detects this mismatch.

For every caller and ether amount, when the contract has a positive balance the owner can always call withdrawAll successfully (making address(c).balance == 0); the mutant inverting onlyOwner can let a non-owner succeed while the owner fails, violating this property for some fuzzed caller/address and amount.

For any caller and any positive deposit amount, the original contract guarantees that the owner can always call withdrawAll successfully (call does not revert) and thus withdraws funds; the mutant inverts onlyOwner so there exist caller addresses for which the owner cannot call withdrawAll (it reverts) while that non-owner can, violating this rule.

For every caller address and positive contract balance, calling withdrawAll as the contract owner always succeeds (does not revert) and leaves the contract balance at 0; the mutant inverts onlyOwner so there exist callers for which the owner call reverts (or does not withdraw) while a non-owner could succeed, violating this rule.

For any caller address and any deposited positive ether amount, when the contract balance is positive the owner can always call withdrawAll successfully (call returns / does not revert) — the mutant inverts onlyOwner so there exist inputs where the owner cannot call withdrawAll but a non-owner can, violating this rule.

For all callers and amounts, only the deployer (owner) can cause contract balance to decrease via withdrawAll; the mutant removing the onlyOwner check allows some non-owner caller to withdraw and thus reduce address(c).balance.

For any caller who is the stored owner and any withdraw amount <= contract balance, after withdraw(...) the contract balance decreases by that amount (reference) — the mutant that always pays payable(owner) can fail this when the caller is a different address set as owner via constructor caller differences, so the balance delta rule is violated for some inputs.

For any caller who is the contract owner and any withdraw amount <= contract balance, after withdraw(amount) the contract's balance decreases by exactly amount (reference sends to msg.sender, mutant sends to stored owner which can keep funds in contract when owner==address(this) or misroute), but the mutant can violate this for some caller/owner relation and amount.

For any caller (fuzzed) who is the contract owner and any withdraw amount ≤ contract balance, calling withdraw(amount) on the reference will succeed (not revert) and reduce address(c).balance by exactly amount; the mutant that always transfers to the stored owner can cause the call to still succeed but not reduce c's balance when the stored owner equals the contract itself or otherwise divert funds, violating the balance-change rule for some inputs.

For any address caller who is the contract owner and any withdraw amount <= contract balance, calling withdraw(amount) transfers the withdrawn ETH to the caller (msg.sender) so the caller's balance increases by amount; the mutant that always transfers to stored owner breaks this when owner != msg.sender (some inputs).

For any caller who is the contract owner and any withdraw amount <= contract balance, withdraw(amount) always sends the funds to the caller (msg.sender) — the mutant that sends to stored owner instead can cause the caller not to receive the funds for some inputs (when owner != msg.sender).

For any caller and any amount, calling withdraw on the correct contract always reduces the contract balance by exactly the withdrawn amount (i.e., address(c).balance decreases by _value when owner withdraws _value); the mutant using call can fail to transfer funds when the recipient's fallback reverts, causing a different post-call contract balance for some inputs.

For any caller and any value, when the owner calls withdraw(_value) the reference contract always decreases its balance by _value (the transfer to owner cannot fail), whereas the mutant that uses low-level call can fail when the recipient reverts, leaving the contract balance unchanged for some inputs.

For any owner-invoked withdraw(amount) the reference contract always reduces its own balance by amount (transfer to owner cannot fail), while the mutant using low-level call can leave the contract balance unchanged when the recipient reverts, so there exist inputs (an adversarial recipient and amount) where the mutant does not reduce address(c).balance by amount.

For any owner-triggered withdraw(amount) where the recipient's fallback does NOT revert, both reference and mutant succeed; but there exists an adversarial recipient whose fallback reverts causing the mutant (which uses low-level call and checks the boolean) to revert while the reference (using transfer) would still revert as well — instead, target a difference in gas stipend: transfer uses 2300 gas and will revert if recipient needs more, whereas the mutant forwards all gas; therefore the general rule: when the recipient deliberately consumes more than 2300 gas in its fallback, the reference's transfer will revert (making withdraw fail) but the mutant's call will succeed — we assert that for any non-adversarial recipient (a simple payable receiver that does minimal work) withdraw succeeds, i.e., calling withdraw as owner to that benign recipient always results in a successful transfer (no revert) — the mutant breaks this by changing failure semantics for adversarial recipients that require >2300 gas.

For any owner-invoked withdraw(amount) where the recipient is a simple contract whose fallback always accepts funds (does not revert) and does only minimal work, the call from C to transfer funds always succeeds and reduces C's balance by the amount (so withdraw returns/does not revert); the mutant using low-level call can behave differently when the recipient intentionally reverts — therefore deploying a benign receiver that accepts funds ensures the reference's withdraw always succeeds for all fuzzed amounts, while the mutant will also succeed for that benign receiver but will fail for a reverter; we instead assert that when the owner calls withdraw to a benign receiver after funding C, the transaction succeeds (no revert) for all amounts — the mutant breaks neutrality in other cases but will still pass here, so to distinguish we use a ReentrantReceiver that in its fallback consumes >2300 gas causing transfer to revert on the reference but call to succeed — thus the general rule used: withdraw to a receiver that tries to consume >2300 gas in fallback will revert on the reference (transfer) but succeed on the mutant (call), so we assert the opposite: for any owner and amount, calling withdraw to a reentrant/gas-consuming receiver causes the reference to revert (ok==false), a behavior the mutant will violate (ok==true) for some inputs.

For any target address and value, when the owner calls sendMoney forwarding X wei, the reference contract transfers that X out of C (reducing address(c).balance accordingly); the mutant that forces value=0 breaks this by leaving address(c).balance unchanged for some nonzero X and a payable target that accepts the funds.

For any nonzero amount and a callee that accepts ETH, calling sendMoney forwards that exact amount out of the contract (reducing address(c).balance); the mutant that forces value=0 leaves the contract balance unchanged for some nonzero amounts and an accepting callee.

For all callers and inputs, only the owner can change contract state via sendMoney (so depositsCount and contract balance change only when called by the owner); the mutant removing the ownership check allows a non-owner to call sendMoney and thus change contract state for some inputs.

For every caller and calldata/value, only the owner may cause C's external call via sendMoney to execute and thereby potentially change depositsCount or balances; the mutant removing the ownership check allows a non-owner caller (an adversarial contract) to invoke sendMoney and change C's state for some fuzzed inputs, violating the rule.

For all callers and inputs, only the owner can cause sendMoney to be executed and thus change the contract's state (so calling sendMoney from non-owner addresses should not alter C's depositsCount); removing the onlyOwner check allows a non-owner adversarial contract to invoke sendMoney and change depositsCount for some fuzzed inputs, breaking this rule.

For all callers and calldata/values, only the owner can cause sendMoney to execute and thereby change C.depositCount or C.balance; removing the onlyOwner check allows a non-owner adversarial contract to call sendMoney and change C's state for some fuzzed inputs.

For every caller address and calldata/value, only the owner can successfully invoke sendMoney (so a non-owner call to sendMoney will not change address(c).balance); removing the onlyOwner check allows a non-owner adversarial contract to call sendMoney and thus change address(c).balance for some fuzzed inputs.
